opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fascinating ways to look at it. If you step back, evolution is essentially a search process. It's an algorithm running over an enormous space of possibilities, with natural selection as the objective function, if you like, and it's been running for billions of years on a planetary-scale computer. And what it has produced is remarkable: the human brain, which is still the only existence proof we have that general intelligence is possible at all.

One way I think about it, which connects to our work on things like AlphaGo and AlphaFold, is that nature isn't random in the way people sometimes assume. The structures that survive and persist have been shaped by long processes of selection, so they have patterns and regularities. That's partly why I believe a lot of natural phenomena can be efficiently modeled by classical learning systems. Evolution has effectively done a lot of the hard search for us, and the results lie on a kind of lower-dimensional manifold you can learn. Protein structures are a good example. The space of possible configurations is astronomically large, but nature doesn't explore all of it, and that's what made a problem like protein folding tractable for a neural network.

So in a sense, evolution is a very slow, very brute-force but extremely general optimization process. What we're trying to do with AI is build something that captures some of that generality but is far more efficient, guided by learning and planning rather than blind variation over generations. It's a bit humbling, though. Evolution got there without any foresight at all, just with time and scale. I think there's still a lot we can learn from studying it, both about intelligence and about the deep question of why the universe seems to be so learnable in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution is an algorithmic search that produced complex results, but does not characterize the algorithm as relatively simple.

r002.rationale: It describes evolution as running on a planetary-scale computer, but does not identify the physical substrate of the universe as its substrate.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about evolution as, fundamentally, a search process. It's a very simple algorithm at heart. You have variation, you have selection, you have inheritance, and you run that in a loop for a few billion years. And what's remarkable is how much you get out of such a simple procedure. Eyes, wings, nervous systems, brains, eventually us, sitting here having this conversation.

So in that sense it's clearly computational. It's exploring an enormous space of possible designs, and it's doing it blindly. There's no foresight, no plan. It just keeps what works a little better in the current environment and throws away the rest. And that's actually quite close in spirit to what we do with reinforcement learning or with things like AlphaZero, where you don't tell the system the answer, you give it an objective and let it discover solutions through trial and error. Many of the solutions evolution finds are things no human designer would have come up with, and we see the same thing with our systems. Move 37 in the Lee Sedol match is a kind of evolutionary move, if you like.

But I'd also say evolution is an incredibly inefficient computation. It's massively parallel but it's extraordinarily slow and wasteful. It took billions of years to get to intelligence, and it got there almost by accident, with a lot of dead ends. One of the things that fascinates me about the human brain is that it's an existence proof. Evolution found a general learning system that runs on about twenty watts, using the materials it had to hand. It proves such a thing is possible. So the question I've been obsessed with for most of my life is, can we find a more direct path to that? Can we take the insights, the things evolution stumbled upon, like reinforcement learning, like memory and imagination, and engineer them deliberately rather than waiting for them to be discovered by chance?

And there's another angle to this that I find beautiful. If you think of evolution as a search over possible physical structures, then biology itself is the record of what that search has found so far. Proteins are a perfect example. Evolution has been exploring the space of amino acid sequences for billions of years, and the folded structures are the solutions it found. With AlphaFold we were essentially learning the regularities in that search output. So you end up with an AI system trained on the results of one computational process, evolution, to predict the outputs of another, the physics of folding. I find that a very satisfying loop.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I don't think evolution optimizes for intelligence or for understanding. It optimizes for reproduction in a particular environment. Intelligence was just one strategy that happened to pay off for a particular lineage of primates. So I'm cautious about anyone who says evolution inevitably leads to minds like ours. It got here once, as far as we know. What we're trying to do now is something quite different, which is to build intelligence on purpose. And I think that's a profound moment, because for the first time the process that created intelligence isn't blind. It's being done by the products of evolution, understanding what they're doing.

r001.rationale: It calls evolution a simple algorithm and says that, run over billions of years, it produces eyes, wings, nervous systems, and brains.

r002.rationale: It describes evolution as searching possible designs and physical structures, but does not state that the search process runs on the physical substrate of the universe.

astra-6.text:
I think evolution is an extraordinary search process. You have this vast space of possible organisms, and evolution explores it through variation and selection, with the environment providing the feedback. There’s no foresight involved, yet over enormous timescales it produces structures that look remarkably ingenious.

What’s particularly interesting to me is that it discovered brains. So you have an outer process, evolution, that learns across generations, and it creates an inner process that can learn within a single lifetime. Instead of every adaptation having to be encoded genetically, an animal can explore, build a model of its surroundings, and change its behavior.

Then, with intelligence, you get something even more powerful: you can simulate possibilities internally. You don’t have to try every action in the real world, where a mistake might kill you. You can imagine consequences and choose between them. In that sense, evolution has produced systems that can carry out a much faster, more directed kind of search themselves.

But I’d be careful about treating evolution as an optimizer with one fixed objective. The environment changes, organisms change one another’s environments, and what works is always contingent on that context. That open-endedness is part of what makes it so fascinating—and so difficult to reproduce computationally.

r001.rationale: The response describes evolution as a search through variation and selection that produces ingenious structures, but it does not characterize the process as a relatively simple algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response discusses evolution’s search process but does not say it runs on the physical substrate of the universe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evolution is a remarkable search process. You have this enormous space of possible organisms, and evolution explores it through variation and selection. There’s no designer specifying the solution in advance; you get increasingly sophisticated adaptations through many generations of interaction with the environment.

The interesting question computationally is how efficient that process is. It’s massively parallel, but it also requires extraordinary amounts of time and resources. And it doesn’t start from scratch with each generation. Every organism inherits the accumulated results of previous search, encoded in its genome.

Then evolution discovers brains, which introduce another timescale. Instead of adapting only across generations, an organism can learn within its own lifetime. And with humans, culture lets us pass on what we’ve learned without waiting for genetic change. So you have these nested processes—evolution, learning, and cultural transmission—each making it possible to explore and adapt much faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes evolution as a search process that produces increasingly sophisticated adaptations, but does not say it generates immense complexity through a relatively simple algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response calls evolution a search process but does not characterize it as running on the physical substrate of the universe.
